theme: Quitting and cutting down: recovery timeline, risk by years since quitting, life regained, reduction and relapse

models.name: Since your last cigarette: recovery milestones
models.estimates: What improves, and roughly when, after stopping smoking.

inputs.name: last_cigarette_datetime
inputs.how_we_get_it: one-time question / quit button in app

table.milestone: heart rate and blood pressure drop
carbon monoxide level in blood drops to normal
circulation improves and lung function increases
coughing and shortness of breath decrease
coronary heart disease risk about half that of a smoker
stroke risk reduced to that of a non-smoker
lung cancer risk about half that of a smoker; risk of mouth, throat, oesophagus, bladder, cervix and pancreas cancer decreases
coronary heart disease risk that of a non-smoker

valid_for.population: WHO summary of the literature (mainly US Surgeon General reports)

models.uncertainty: No CIs; population-average statements. Some milestones are optimistic compared with newer cohort data (see quitting-cvd-by-years-heavy-smokers and quitting-lung-cancer-by-years): heavy smokers' excess risk can last longer.

source.citation: World Health Organization. Tobacco: health benefits of smoking cessation (Questions and answers), 25 February 2020
source.where: 'Beneficial health changes that take place' list
source.quote: 12 hours, the carbon monoxide level in your blood drops to normal.

supporting_sources.citation: WHO Europe news release, 29 Sep 2020 (Tobacco Knowledge Summary on coronary heart disease)

models.caveats: You asked for each milestone with its own primary source: the WHO page lists references (e.g. Mahmud & Feely, Hypertension 2003 for the 20-minute item; US Surgeon General reports) but I did not open them individually in this pass. Treat as an authoritative summary, not per-milestone primary evidence. The same WHO list is widely copied by quit apps; use the WHO page as your citation, not the apps.
models.user_copy: {elapsed} since your last cigarette: {milestone}. Keep going — the biggest gains come over months and years.

models.name: Life expectancy not lost, per cigarette not smoked
models.estimates: Minutes of life expectancy avoided losing since quitting (or from cigarettes cut), based on the per-cigarette loss estimate.

inputs.name: cigs_not_smoked
inputs.how_we_get_it: (pre-quit daily average from log) × days since quit, or reduction vs baseline

table.paper_says: a full day of life by 8 January, a week by 20 February, a month by 5 August, 50 days by end of year

valid_for.exposure_range: population average; assumes the cigarettes would otherwise have been smoked for life

models.uncertainty: No CI; arithmetic estimate. The paper's own worked example matches the formula (10 × 20 × 365 ≈ 50.7 days).

source.citation: Jackson SE, Jarvis MJ, West R. The price of a cigarette: 20 minutes of life? Addiction 2025;120(5):810-812
source.quote: a person smoking 10 cigarettes per day who quits smoking on the 1st of January 2025 could prevent loss of a full day of life by the 8th of January, a week of life by the 20th of February, and a month by the 5th of August. By the end of the year, they could have avoided losing 50 days of life.

models.caveats: Using it for cutting down (not quitting) is weaker: the paper itself warns reduced smokers may inhale more deeply per cigarette, and heart risk barely falls with cutting down (see cutting-down-cvd). For bidis or chewing tobacco there is no per-unit figure — do not apply.
models.user_copy: By not smoking {n} cigarettes, you've avoided losing about {days} days of life expectancy (population average).

models.name: Years of life regained by age at quitting
models.estimates: Average life expectancy gained by stopping at a given age, compared with continuing to smoke.
models.output_unit: years of life expectancy vs continuing smokers

valid_for.exposure_range: former cigarette smokers who had smoked about as much as continuing smokers

models.uncertainty: No CIs; read from survival curves (Figure 4). Some reverse causation (people quitting because ill) makes later-age estimates conservative.

source.citation: Doll R, Peto R, Boreham J, Sutherland I. Mortality in relation to smoking: 50 years' observations on male British doctors. BMJ 2004;328:1519
source.quote: Cessation at age 60, 50, 40, or 30 years gained, respectively, about 3, 6, 9, or 10 years of life expectancy.

supporting_sources.citation: Jha P, Ramasundarahettige C, Landsman V, et al. 21st-century hazards of smoking and benefits of cessation in the United States. N Engl J Med 2013;368:341-50
supporting_sources.note: US, both sexes: quitting at 25–34, 35–44, 45–54 gained about 10, 9 and 6 years; cessation before 40 reduces the excess death risk of continued smoking by about 90%. (A 55–64 → 4 years figure appears in secondary reports; not verified in the abstract read.)

supporting_sources.citation: WHO. Tobacco: health benefits of smoking cessation (2020)

models.caveats: Show as 'quitting at any age helps', with the age row closest to the user. No Indian estimate found; the direction is expected to hold.
models.user_copy: People who quit around age {age} gained on average about {years} years of life compared with those who kept smoking.

models.name: How much of the extra death risk is avoided, by age at quitting (women)
models.estimates: Relative risk of death (and of lung cancer death) for ex-smokers vs never smokers by age at stopping, and the share of smokers' excess risk avoided.

valid_for.population: UK Million Women Study, recruited 1996–2001, followed to 2011

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. The <25 group is small (24 lung cancer deaths) and the authors call it not statistically trustworthy.

source.citation: Pirie K, Peto R, Reeves GK, Green J, Beral V; Million Women Study Collaborators. The 21st century hazards of smoking and benefits of stopping: a prospective study of one million women in the UK. Lancet 2013;381(9861):133-141
source.quote: Stopping before age 40 years (and preferably well before age 40 years) avoids more than 90% of the excess mortality caused by continuing smoking; stopping before age 30 years avoids more than 97% of it.

supporting_sources.citation: Banks E et al. BMC Med 2019;17:128 (Australia)
supporting_sources.note: CVD risks in those who quit before 35 did not differ significantly from never smokers; quitting by 35–44 avoided about 90% of excess CVD risk.

models.caveats: The paper stresses it is not 'safe to smoke until 40 then stop': those who did still had 1.2 times the death rate decades later. Use for motivation ('the earlier the better'), not as permission.
models.user_copy: Quitting before 40 avoids about 90% of smoking's extra death risk; before 30, about 97%. It's never too late — even quitting around 50 avoids about two-thirds.

models.name: Heart and stroke risk by years since quitting (heavy smokers)
models.estimates: Incident cardiovascular disease (MI, stroke, heart failure, CVD death) rate and hazard in former heavy smokers by years since quitting, vs current and never smokers.

valid_for.population: USA, Framingham Heart Study original + offspring cohorts, 1954–2015; mostly white

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Time course differed by cohort (5–10 years original, ≥25 years offspring).

source.citation: Duncan MS, Freiberg MS, Greevy RA Jr, Kundu S, Vasan RS, Tindle HA. Association of smoking cessation with subsequent risk of cardiovascular disease. JAMA 2019;322(7):642-650
source.quote: quitting within 5 years was associated with significantly lower rates of incident CVD (incidence rates per 1000 person-years: current smoking, 11.56 [95% CI, 10.30-12.98]; quitting within 5 years, 6.94 [95% CI, 5.61-8.59]

supporting_sources.citation: Teo KK et al. INTERHEART, Lancet 2006
supporting_sources.note: Heart attack OR for former smokers 1.87 (1.55–2.24) within 3 years of quitting and 1.22 (1.09–1.37) 20+ years after (vs 2.95 current).

models.caveats: Volume/page numbers (322(7):642-650) are from my memory and not visible in the page read — verify. Applies to ≥20 pack-years; lighter smokers likely recover faster but that is not in this model.
models.user_copy: Within 5 years of quitting, heart and stroke risk drops by about 40% (range 24–51%) compared with continuing to smoke.

models.name: Lung cancer risk by years since quitting (heavy smokers)
models.estimates: Hazard of lung cancer in former heavy smokers vs never smokers, by years since quitting.

valid_for.population: USA, Framingham Heart Study, median follow-up 28.7 years
valid_for.exposure_range: heavy former smokers (≥21 pack-years per paper's definition; not visible in the abstract snippet — verify)

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed and wide (284 lung cancers total).

source.citation: Tindle HA, Stevenson Duncan M, Greevy RA, et al. Lifetime smoking history and risk of lung cancer: results from the Framingham Heart Study. J Natl Cancer Inst 2018
source.quote: Heavy former (vs current) smokers had 39.1% lower lung cancer risk within five YSQ.

supporting_sources.citation: Cancer risk following smoking cessation in Korea (JAMA Netw Open, PMC10848071)
supporting_sources.note: Asian cohort of >2 million: all-cancer risk slightly higher for ~10 years after quitting (likely sick-quitters), then fell to ~50% of continuing smokers after 15+ years; lung cancer fell ~3 years earlier; quitting before 50 gave lung cancer HR 0.43 (0.35–0.53). Key-points level only.
Lung cancer RR vs never by age stopped: 1.84 (25–34), 3.34 (35–44), 5.91 (45–54) vs 24.0 continuing.

models.caveats: Honest message: lung cancer risk falls a lot compared with continuing, but stays above never-smokers for decades — which is why lung screening eligibility lasts 15 years after quitting (H1 pack-years model). Frame vs 'if you had kept smoking', not vs never-smokers, to avoid discouraging quitters.
models.user_copy: Within 5 years of quitting, lung cancer risk is about 40% lower than if you'd kept smoking, and it keeps falling for decades.

models.name: Cutting down by half: lung cancer
models.estimates: Lung cancer hazard for heavy smokers (≥15/day) who cut down by at least 50%, vs those who kept smoking heavily, alongside quitters and never smokers.

inputs.name: baseline_cigs_per_day
inputs.how_we_get_it: first 30 days of log or one-time question

models.output_unit: hazard ratio vs persistent heavy smokers

valid_for.population: Denmark, three Copenhagen cohorts, 19,714 people, up to 31 years' follow-up

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed; reducers' CI close to 1 (0.54–0.98).

source.citation: Godtfredsen NS, Prescott E, Osler M. Effect of smoking reduction on lung cancer risk. JAMA 2005;294(12):1505-1510
source.quote: the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for lung cancer in reducers was 0.73 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.54-0.98) compared with persistent heavy smokers.

supporting_sources.note: Reducers ≥50%: lung cancer aHR 0.83 (0.77–0.88) vs sustainers; quitters 0.79 (0.76–0.83). See also cutting-down-and-relapse-cancer.

models.caveats: Show next to cutting-down-cvd: cutting down helps lung cancer somewhat, but quitting helps far more and the heart barely benefits from cutting down.
models.user_copy: Cutting down by half lowered lung cancer risk by about a quarter (range 2–46%). Quitting halves it and keeps lowering it.

models.name: Cutting down vs quitting: heart and stroke
models.estimates: Relative risk of heart disease / CVD in heavy smokers who cut down substantially vs continuing heavy smokers, compared with quitters, in three cohorts.
models.output_unit: relative risk vs continuing heavy smokers (CIs not reported in the text read)

valid_for.population: Denmark, Norway, South Korea cohorts as summarised
valid_for.exposure_range: heavy smokers reducing by about half or more

models.uncertainty: Values are as summarised in the meta-analysis discussion, without CIs; the original cohort papers were not opened.

source.citation: Hackshaw A, Morris JK, Boniface S, Tang JL, Milenković D. Low cigarette consumption and risk of coronary heart disease and stroke: meta-analysis of 141 cohort studies in 55 study reports. BMJ 2018;360:j5855
source.quote: The adjusted relative risk for cardiovascular disease after 21 years' follow-up was 1.02 (compared with continuing heavy smokers), unlike the benefit seen in quitters (relative risk 0.46)

models.caveats: This is the key honest message for the 'cut down' screen: cutting down barely lowers heart/stroke risk (consistent with the steep-then-flat dose curve in H1 smoking-dose-chd). If you want to show numbers from the original Danish/Norwegian/Korean papers with CIs, those need to be opened separately.
models.user_copy: Cutting down helps your lungs a bit, but your heart mostly benefits only when you stop completely.

models.name: Cutting down, quitting and going back to smoking: cancer risk (Korea)
models.estimates: Cancer hazards for reducers and quitters vs sustained smokers, and for people who resumed smoking vs those who stayed quit.

inputs.name: relapsed_after_quit
inputs.how_we_get_it: log shows cigarettes after a quit date

table.group: reducer who then quit vs sustainer
resumed smoking (even at lower level) vs stayed quit

valid_for.population: South Korea, 893,582 smokers screened 2009 and 2011 (682,996 also 2013), followed to 2018

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Short follow-up (≤9 years) for cancer, so long-term differences may be larger.

source.citation: Yoo JE, Han K, Shin DW, et al. Effect of smoking reduction, cessation, and resumption on cancer risk: a nationwide cohort study. Cancer 2022;128(11):2126-2137
source.quote: Smoking resumption after quitting, even at a lower level, increased the risk of smoking-related cancers (aHR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.06-1.33) and lung cancer (aHR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.21-1.80) in comparison with sustained quitting.

models.caveats: Answers 'does relapse reset benefits?' only partly: relapse raised cancer risk vs staying quit, but the study doesn't say risk returns fully to pre-quit level. One abstract CI looks mistyped (smoking-related cancers for reducer-then-quit printed as 0.81 (0.81–0.92)); not used here. Relapse copy must be kind: a slip is not failure, re-quitting restores benefit.
models.user_copy: Slipped back? It happens. Going back to smoking raised lung cancer risk by about 1.5 times compared with staying quit — quitting again gets you back on track.

models.name: Type 2 diabetes risk after quitting (temporary rise, then fall)
models.estimates: Relative risk of type 2 diabetes in former smokers by years since quitting, vs never smokers.
models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Current-smoker row from the same meta-analysis (88 studies).

source.citation: Pan A, Wang Y, Talaei M, Hu FB, Wu T. Relation of active, passive, and quitting smoking with incident type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2015;3(12):958-67
source.quote: the pooled RR from ten studies with 1 086 608 participants was 1·54 (95% CI 1·36-1·74) for new quitters (<5 years), 1·18 (1·07-1·29) for middle-term quitters (5-9 years), and 1·11 (1·02-1·20) for long-term quitters (≥10 years).

models.caveats: Important for a calorie app: the early rise is linked to weight gain after quitting. Pair with Prana's food/activity features ('watch weight in the first years after quitting') rather than scaring people off quitting. Weight-gain numbers are planned for H5.
models.user_copy: Diabetes risk can rise a little in the first few years after quitting (often from weight gain), then falls. Keeping an eye on food and activity now helps.

not_found.reason: WHO page cites them (e.g. Mahmud & Feely 2003; US Surgeon General reports) but I did not open each one in this pass.

not_found.reason: Not searched in this pass; oral-cancer risk reversal after quitting betel quid (Gupta R et al., Ann Glob Health 2022, cited in the H1-2 oral cancer paper) is the next source.

not_found.reason: Only Yoo 2022 (relapse vs sustained quitting) found; no source quantifies relapse vs never having quit.

recommend: Show first: (1) quitting-minutes-regained — a live, motivating counter from day 1, same source as H1, with the paper's own worked example as a test case. (2) quitting-recovery-timeline — the standard 'since your last cigarette' screen, cited to WHO (not the apps that copy it). (3) quitting-cvd-by-years-heavy-smokers and quitting-lung-cancer-by-years — honest curves: big drop within 5 years vs continuing, full recovery takes longer. (4) cutting-down-lung-cancer + cutting-down-cvd side by side — tells 'cutters' the truth kindly: good first step, but the heart needs a full quit. (5) cutting-down-and-relapse-cancer for relapse copy. Already in earlier files and reusable on the quit screen: oral/pharyngeal cancer halves within ~10 years (H1-2), pancreas 0.6 after 20 years (H1-2), gum disease quitters = never smokers (H1-2), dementia former smokers RR 1.01 (H1-2), INTERHEART former smokers 1.87 → 1.22 (H2).
